svg.title: Figure 1. Three places a password vault can live, and what each means
svg.desc: Three architectures compared. Local first keeps the encrypted file on your own machines and you arrange synchronisation. A vendor service holds the encrypted vault for you. Self-hosting puts the service on infrastructure you run. Each is assessed on who holds a copy, what a breach of that holder yields, and what you have to do yourself. A band below states the point that unites them: once somebody holds a copy of your encrypted vault, the only thing between them and its contents is your master password and the work factor protecting it.
svg.text: Figure 1: Who Ends Up Holding a Copy
The architectures differ less than they appear. What differs is how many parties end up with an encrypted copy of everything you have.

svg.text: What all three have in common, and it is the thing that matters
Once anybody holds a copy of your encrypted vault, the only things between them and its contents are your master password and the work factor protecting it.
They can attack it offline, at their own pace, with no rate limit and nobody to notice. That is true of a file on a sync service exactly as it is true of a vendor breach.
So the architecture decision is smaller than it looks, and the master password and key derivation settings are larger.
Guidance that says "the file is already encrypted, so cloud sync is fine" is stating the premise of the attack as though it were the answer to it.
